common_name: Silk Tassel Sedge (Fine-Leaved Variegated Japanese Sedge)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring or early fall into humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; give the clump a season to settle before expecting its full cascading habit.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where this Japanese sedge selection forms a relaxed, fountain-like mound of extremely narrow blades striped green and white. Collected in Japan in 1970, 'Silk Tassel' is prized for foliage far finer-textured than typical Carex morrowii cultivars, giving it a soft, shimmering quality when it catches breeze or low light. It is evergreen in mild climates and holds its variegation without scorching even in fairly deep shade, making it a good choice near the base of trees or along a shaded path where finer detail can be appreciated up close. Site it beside rocks, at a pond edge, or massed as a woodland-floor accent, and divide congested clumps in spring every three to four years to maintain vigor.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; shear old foliage to the ground in early spring before new growth emerges to keep the fresh white coloring unmarred.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; 'Snow Cap' is a slow, rhizome-spreading selection of broad-leaved sedge whose wide blades emerge in spring almost entirely creamy white, developing thin, irregular dark green striping as the season progresses — essentially the color reverse of the older 'Variegata' cultivar. The low, mounding habit stays under a foot tall, making it useful as a bright accent at the front of a shaded border or woven through a shade groundcover planting where its pale color reads from a distance even in dim light. It is just as deer- and rabbit-resistant as other broad-leaved sedges despite carrying so little chlorophyll in the leaf. Divide congested clumps in early spring or early fall, and keep soil consistently moist during the first year to help new divisions establish before they begin spreading.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; remote sedge self-sows modestly once established and will fill in bare damp ground under trees.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; remote sedge is a European woodland native named for its widely spaced flower spikes, which nod along slender arching stems above loose, delicate, glossy bright-green tufts. It is among the most reliably shade-loving of all garden sedges, thriving in the damp, dim conditions found along streambanks, in low woodland hollows, and beside shaded water features where many other ornamental grasses fail. Full hot sun bleaches the foliage toward yellow-green, so siting it out of direct afternoon exposure preserves the deep color that makes it such an effective foil for hostas, ferns, and other broad-leaved shade perennials. It self-sows lightly in favorable damp sites, gradually forming a loose colony without becoming aggressive, and clumps can be lifted and divided in early summer if propagation is desired.
sources: British Society of Britain & Ireland (BSBI) Plant Atlas

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist to average, well-drained soil in partial shade; cut the evergreen clump to the ground in late winter each year to force fresh, brightly striped spring foliage.

directions: Plant in moist to average, well-drained soil in partial shade; 'Moonraker' is a variegated sport of the large, weeping pendulous sedge, discovered in a Wiltshire hedgerow and shared by UK grass breeder Roger Grounds in the late 1990s. New spring foliage emerges heavily streaked white before gradually fading toward green over the season, so the display is most dramatic if the clump is cut hard to the ground in late winter to force an entirely fresh flush of striped leaves. Tall, arching flower stems carry long, dangling catkin-like spikes above the foliage mound in early summer, adding movement and texture even after the variegation has faded. It tolerates a wide range of soils from constantly moist to surprisingly dry once established, but the boldest color and largest habit come with reliable moisture and shelter from the hottest afternoon sun. Useful as a large accent at the shaded margin of a pond or woodland border where its scale and weeping form can stand out.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; this variegated selection is slower to bulk up than the straight species, so allow extra time for the clump to reach full size.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; 'Shade Fanfare' is a variegated selection of the native plantain-leaved sedge, its broad, softly pleated leaves edged in creamy white around a deep green center, giving the mound a brighter presence than the species in the dim light under mature trees. Burgundy-toned flower stems emerge in early spring before the new leaves fully unfurl, adding a subtle seasonal accent to what is primarily a foliage plant. The wide leaf form is distinct from most narrow-bladed sedges and pairs especially well with ferns, hellebores, and other fine-textured woodland companions that benefit from the contrast. It is semi-evergreen in milder climates and slow but steady to spread, forming a tidy, long-lived clump rather than an aggressive groundcover, and rarely needs division except to propagate new plants.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into average to rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; it also tolerates more sun than most broad-leaved sedges if soil moisture stays consistent.

directions: Plant in average to rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to mostly shade; 'Shima-nishiki,' sold in the US as Island Brocade Sedge, carries broad grassy leaves with cream-streaked lime-green centers and gold margins, making it one of the most colorful of the broad-leaved sedges. The low mound spreads gradually by rhizomes into a dense, weed-suppressing patch, useful as an edging along shaded paths or as a bright groundcover beneath shrubs and small trees. Its tricolor variegation holds up well through summer heat where soil moisture is dependable, fading only if the site turns hot and dry for extended periods. Like its relatives, it is rarely bothered by deer or rabbits, and old foliage can be trimmed back in early spring before new growth emerges to keep the clump looking fresh. It combines nicely near water features or in low, moist spots where its color can be appreciated up close.
